turns.text: Can you describe what it felt like the very first morning you woke up in the countryside after leaving Shanghai?

The first morning, I woke up on a hard wooden plank, not a bed, and my neck ached from the unfamiliar pillow stuffed with husks. My breath came out in a cloud, and the air in the room was colder than anything I’d felt inside a house in Shanghai. I could smell damp earth and something sour, maybe from the boots lined up by the door. The others were already moving, pulling on thick, stiff jackets and wrapping scarves around their heads. I heard the wind outside, sharp and endless, and I knew there would be no warm breakfast waiting—just a bowl of thin corn gruel and a piece of steamed bread, if I was lucky. My hands shook as I dressed, not just from the cold but from the sense that nothing familiar would be returning. The silence between the women, the way we avoided each other’s eyes, made it clear: everyone was pretending not to be afraid, but I could feel fear sitting right next to me, heavy as another person.

You describe the silence between the women and the way everyone avoided each other's eyes—it's striking how fear seemed to fill the room. Did you find ways to connect with any of the others in those early days, or did that sense of distance linger?

At first, the distance lingered. We were all from different neighborhoods in Shanghai, and none of us wanted to look weak. But after a few days of working in the fields, shoveling frozen earth side by side, something shifted. One evening, my hands were so cracked they bled, and I couldn’t hold my chopsticks. Without a word, the girl next to me tore her steamed bread in half and pushed the bigger piece toward me. It was a small gesture, but in that moment, I felt seen. Later, when I tried to wash my clothes at the pump and couldn’t break the ice in the basin, another girl helped me smash it with a rock. Little things like that—sharing food, helping with chores—became our way of speaking when we couldn’t say what we really felt. We didn’t talk about home, but sometimes, late at night, someone would hum a tune from the city, and the rest of us would listen in the dark. That was how we started to connect: quietly, through actions more than words.

It’s powerful how you describe connection growing out of necessity and small acts, rather than conversation. When someone hummed a tune from the city at night, what kinds of feelings did that bring up for you?

When I heard those tunes, something inside me tightened and ached at the same time. The melody would drift over the room, so faint I sometimes wondered if I imagined it. It made me remember the sound of trams rattling past my old apartment window, the way my sisters argued over the radio dial, the smell of fried dough from the street stalls. For a few minutes, I felt both closer to home and farther away than ever. The music made me want to cry, but I never did—crying felt dangerous, like it might open a flood I couldn’t stop. Instead, I lay there listening, holding the tune in my mind until sleep finally pulled me under. It was a reminder that I hadn’t disappeared, that the city was still part of me even though I was swallowed up by fields and cold. But it also hurt, because I knew I couldn’t go back—not really, not as the person I was before.

Your memory of lying awake, holding onto those city tunes in the dark, really captures how homesickness and hope can mix together. You mentioned that crying felt dangerous, like it might unleash something uncontrollable—did you ever see anyone else break down, or was everyone determined to keep their feelings hidden?

One night, when the wind was howling so loud it rattled the window frames, I heard muffled sobs from the corner of the room. I didn’t look over; none of us did. The crying was quiet, but it went on for a long time, broken by hiccups and deep, shaky breaths. In the morning, the girl’s eyes were swollen, but she acted as if nothing had happened, scrubbing her face hard with cold water. No one mentioned it. That was our unspoken rule—you could fall apart a little, as long as you patched yourself together by sunrise. Sometimes, I caught glimpses of someone’s hands trembling or saw someone staring out at the fields with their jaw clenched tight. We all had our moments, but we protected each other’s pain by pretending not to see it.

It’s striking how you all respected each other’s privacy, even in such close quarters. You mentioned scrubbing her face with cold water in the morning—what were mornings like for you after nights like that, when emotions ran high but nothing was spoken?

After a night like that, mornings felt heavier. My body would ache more than usual, and my mind would move slowly, as if I hadn’t really slept. The cold seemed sharper, biting at my cheeks as I washed my face, the water numbing my skin and my thoughts. The silence at breakfast was thicker, every movement—lifting a bowl, breaking bread—deliberate and careful. I watched the steam rise from my gruel and focused on swallowing, just to keep myself anchored in the present. There was no room for softness. I could sense everyone else tightening up, bracing for the day ahead, as if we had to build a shell before stepping outside. The sky was always gray, and the fields stretched out with no end, but we moved through the routine anyway. I felt like I was carrying something under my coat that no one could see, and I knew the others were doing the same.

Your description of building a shell each morning, and carrying something invisible under your coat, makes the emotional weight almost physical. In those moments when you were out in the fields after a difficult night, did the work itself ever help distract you, or did it make the heaviness even harder to shake?

Sometimes the work numbed me, at least for a while. The tasks were so repetitive—lifting, digging, bending, straightening—that my mind would slip into a kind of blankness. My muscles would burn and my breath would fog in the air, and I could almost forget everything except the next movement. But there were other times, especially when my body was exhausted and the wind cut through my jacket, that the heaviness grew worse. The endless rows of frozen earth made me feel small and trapped, and I’d catch myself thinking about Shanghai, about my family, about how far away everything familiar had become. The distraction of work was real, but it never lasted. As soon as I paused, even just to wipe my nose or stretch my back, the ache inside would rush back in, stronger than before.

I can picture the rhythm of that work and how it could dull your thoughts, but also how quickly the ache would return during any pause. You mentioned thinking about your family during those moments—did you ever try to write letters home, and if so, what did you choose to share or keep hidden?

I wrote letters, but every word felt like it had to pass through a filter. I wanted to tell my mother about the cold, about how my hands bled and my stomach never felt full, but I knew she would worry, and I also knew someone else might read what I wrote. I stuck to safe details—describing the fields, the weather, how I was learning to plant and harvest, how I was getting stronger. I asked about my sisters, whether they were behaving, whether the ration lines in Shanghai were any shorter. Sometimes I’d slip in a line about missing home, but I kept it light, almost like a joke. I never mentioned the nights I couldn’t sleep, or the way fear pressed down on me, or the things I saw and heard that made me uneasy. I learned to write around the truth, to make my life sound bearable, even when it wasn’t. Every letter was a performance, and every time I sealed an envelope, I wondered who would really be reading it first.

The idea of writing around the truth, never knowing who might read your words, sounds incredibly lonely. When you received letters back from your family, could you sense them doing the same—hiding their own worries or hardships between the lines?

Yes, I could feel it in every sentence. My mother’s letters were always careful—she wrote about the weather, about neighbors, about little things my sisters did that made her laugh. She told me she was proud, that she hoped I was eating well and making friends. But sometimes her handwriting would waver, or she’d repeat herself, as if she was trying to fill the page without saying too much. She never mentioned how hard it was to get rice, or the arguments in the ration lines, but I knew. She never asked if I was scared or lonely, only if I was “adapting.” Sometimes she would include a proverb or a line from a poem, something about endurance or patience, and I knew that was her way of telling me to hold on. The letters were full of things unsaid, and I read them over and over, trying to hear what she really meant beneath the safe words.

Your description of reading between the lines in your mother’s letters is so vivid—I can imagine how much you must have craved those hidden messages. Was there ever a moment, maybe with a proverb or a small detail, when you suddenly felt a strong connection to home, even from so far away?

Once, my mother ended her letter with a line: “The plum tree survives the winter frost.” She underlined it. I stared at those words for a long time. I could almost see her sitting at our old table, dipping her brush, pausing to think about what she could and couldn’t say. That line was more than advice—it was a promise that she remembered me, that she believed I could survive this cold, both the weather and everything else pressing in. For a moment, I felt the weight of her hand on my shoulder, as if she was right there. I folded the letter and tucked it inside my jacket, over my heart, and carried it with me for weeks. Whenever the wind cut through me or my legs ached so badly I wanted to lie down in the mud, I would touch that spot and repeat her words to myself. It wasn’t the same as being home, but it was enough to keep me moving.

The image of carrying your mother’s letter over your heart, and repeating her words when you needed strength, really stays with me. Looking back now, do you think that kind of quiet support—those hidden messages and small acts—changed how you see family and connection, even years later?
